claims.text: Agra marble inlay combines a marble base with semi-precious stones, and its technique dates back to the Mughal era.

quotes.quote: Agra Marble Inlay is a fine example of craftsmanship, combining the beauty of marble with the allure of semi-precious stones.
Agra Marble Inlay technique is a time-honored art form that dates back to the Mughal era, with a rich tradition of craftsmanship centered around Agra, India.

claims.text: Parchin kari, also called pachhikari or parchinkari, is the art of inlaying coloured or semi-precious stones into a stone base, often in geometric or flower patterns.

quotes.quote: One of them is Parchin Kari or Pachhikari. Parchin Kari is the art of inlaying coloured or semi-precious stones into a stone base, often in geometric or flower patterns.
called parchin kari or parchinkari (Persian: پرچین کاری) in the Indian subcontinent, is a term for the inlay technique of using cut and fitted, highly polished colored stones to create images.

claims.text: In Mughal India pietra dura, adapted into the local Mughal style, came to be known as parchin kari, literally meaning 'driven in'.

quotes.quote: In Mughal India, pietra dura was known as parchin kari, literally 'inlay' or 'driven-in' work.
which had been adapted into the local Mughal style and came to be known as parchin kari, literally meaning 'driven in'.

claims.text: Pietra dura, Italian for 'hard stone', is a technique of cutting, polishing and inlaying precious and semi-precious stones, generally into hard stone such as marble, to represent an image.

quotes.quote: pietra dura, meaning "hard stone" in Italian, is a technique wherein precious and semi-precious stones are cut, polished and inlaid - generally on hard stone, such as marble - to represent an image.
This stonework is generally referred to as pietra dura ("hard stone" in Italian) and known as parchin kari in India.

claims.text: The GI application describes stone inlay, also known as parchin kari, as the most attractive and popular art form of Agra.

quotes.quote: Stone Inlay is also known as Parchin kari which is known as the most attractive and popular forms of Art in Agra.

claims.text: Agra stone inlay work combines carving, inlaying, engraving and sculpture, and the GI application calls Indian marble one of the hardest materials to work.

quotes.quote: As the Indian marble is one of the hardest materials to work, it is not an easy process. This work on stone is a combination of carving, inlaying, engraving and sculpture.

claims.text: The GI application states that parchin kari, the inlay of agate, turquoise, cornelian, jasper, bloodstone, mother of pearl, malachite and lapis lazuli in marble, is unique to Agra.

quotes.quote: Parchin kari or the stone of semi-precious stones - agate, turquoise, cornelian, jasper, bloodstone, mother of pearl, malachite and lapis lazuli in marble is unique to Agra.

claims.text: The GI application says the stone inlay work of Agra reflects the pietra dura mosaic work used in the Taj Mahal and at Fatehpur Sikri.

quotes.quote: The famous stone Inlay work of Agra reflects the mosaic work (Pietra Dura) used in Taj Mahal and Fatehpur Sikri.

claims.text: Agra marble inlay, a tradition of craftsmanship centred around Agra, flourished and reached its peak under the Mughals, especially after the Taj Mahal was built.

quotes.quote: The craft flourished and reached its peak during the era of the Mughals in medieval India and especially after the construction of Taj Mahal.
a rich tradition of craftsmanship centered around Agra, India
Since the time of Shah Jahan, Agra in Uttar Pradesh has remained a thriving centre for marble work, including inlay.
It was made by craftsmen in Agra, a renowned centre for the inlaying of marble with semi-precious stones from the reign of Shah Jahan (r. 1628-1658).

claims.text: The GI application says the sequence of processes was perfected by the artisans in the 17th century and has remained largely unchanged for over 400 years.

quotes.quote: The sequence of processes that culminates in the realization of a masterpiece of marble stone was perfected by the artisans in the 17th century, and has remained largely unchanged for over 400 years.

claims.text: Construction of the Taj Mahal started in 1632; the mausoleum was completed in 1648 and the whole complex in 1653.

quotes.quote: It was built by Mughal Emperor Shah Jahan in memory of his wife Mumtaz Mahal with construction starting in 1632 AD and completed in 1648 AD, with the mosque, the guest house and the main gateway on the south, the outer courtyard and its cloisters were added subsequently and completed in 1653 AD.
Begun in 1632, the entire complex was not completed until 1653

quotes.locator: The Taj Mahal: Pinnacle of Perfection
quotes.quote: The Taj Mahal, built by Shah Jahan in 1632, is the ultimate testament to the brilliance of parchin kari.

claims.text: UNESCO's short description says the Taj Mahal was built in Agra between 1631 and 1648 by order of Shah Jahan.

quotes.quote: An immense mausoleum of white marble, built in Agra between 1631 and 1648 by order of the Mughal emperor Shah Jahan in memory of his favourite wife

claims.text: A design magazine's account of Agra inlay dates the beginning of the Taj Mahal's 17-year construction to 1633.

quotes.quote: they used to be done in 1633, when the 17-year construction of the Taj Mahal began-except that the craft is applied to souvenirs rather than mausoleums these days.

claims.text: Archnet's record of the tomb of Itimad-ud-Daulah dates the beginning of the Taj Mahal's construction to 1630.

quotes.quote: Many of the design elements foreshadow the Taj Mahal, the construction of which began in 1630.

claims.text: More than 20,000 craftsmen and workers are believed to have been employed in building the Taj Mahal.

quotes.quote: It is believed that more than 20,000 artisans, labourers, painters and others were involved in the construction of the building.
is believed to have employed 20,000 laborers
It eventually took more than 1,000 elephants and 20,000 craftsmen from all over Asia to build (Nath, 1985).

claims.text: Inlayers, stone-cutters, carvers and calligraphers for the Taj Mahal were requisitioned from across the empire and from Central Asia and Iran.

quotes.quote: For its construction, masons, stone-cutters, inlayers, carvers, painters, calligraphers, dome builders and other artisans were requisitioned from the whole of the empire and also from the Central Asia and Iran.
the most skilled architects, inlay craftsmen, calligraphers, stone-carvers and masons were called from all across India and lands as distant as Persia and Turkey.

claims.text: Gems & Gemology, citing Havell, says records indicate the parchin kari craftsmen were mostly from Kannauj and were Hindus, not Muslims.

quotes.locator: History of the Families that Performed the Inlay
quotes.quote: Records indicate that the parchin kari craftsmen were mostly from Kannauj and were not Muslim but Hindus (Havell, 2003).

claims.text: Gems & Gemology says that when the Taj Mahal was built parchin kari was used only in the tombs of the emperor's family, and one of the complex's four tombs has a cenotaph so decorated.

quotes.locator: Architecture and Gem Materials of the Taj Mahal
quotes.quote: Two additional tomb buildings, called Saheli Burj, lie along the south end of the complex.

quotes.locator: Architecture and Gem Materials of the Taj Mahal
quotes.quote: One of the four tombs contains a marble cenotaph embellished with parchin kari (this technique was only used in the tombs of the emperor's family at the time the Taj Mahal was built), but vandals have stolen many of the more valuable inlaid stones.

claims.text: Humayun, the second Mughal emperor, is credited with introducing inlay as a significant feature of Mughal architecture.

quotes.locator: From Rome to the Mughal Courts
quotes.quote: Humayun, the second Mughal emperor, is credited with introducing inlay as a significant feature of Mughal architecture.

claims.text: The Qila-i-Kuhna Mosque in Delhi's Purana Qila, of 1540 CE, shows one of the earliest examples of inlay work in India, its mihrab adorned with gold and semi-precious stones.

quotes.locator: From Rome to the Mughal Courts
quotes.quote: The Qila-i-Kuhna Mosque in Delhi's Purana Qila (1540 CE) showcases one of the earliest examples of inlay work in India, with its mihrab adorned with gold and semi-precious stones.

claims.text: The tomb of Itimad-ud-Daulah in Agra is considered the first Mughal structure in India built entirely of white marble.

quotes.quote: The tomb itself is considered the first Mughal structure in India built entirely of white marble.

quotes.locator: The Jewel Box of Mughal India
quotes.quote: It was the first Mughal structure built entirely of white marble, setting the stage for the architectural marvels to come.
The I'timad al-Daula was the first Mughal structure to be completely encased in marble and extensively use pietra dura, the marble inlay work that is associated with the Taj Mahal.

claims.text: Empress Nur Jahan commissioned the tomb of Itimad-ud-Daulah in Agra for her father, and it features geometric designs, flowers and decorated vases in pietra dura.

quotes.quote: The Tomb of Itimad-Ud-Daula, commissioned by Empress Nur Jahan for her father, for instance, features polychromatic geometric designs, flowers and decorated vases using the technique.

quotes.locator: The Jewel Box of Mughal India
quotes.quote: Before the Taj Mahal, the tomb of Itmad-ud-Daula in Agra (1621-1627 CE) marked a turning point in Mughal architecture.
Floral and stylized arabesques, geometrical designs, opus sectile mosaic and pietra dura inlay are used throughout the exterior.

claims.text: The tomb of Itimad-ud-Daulah marks a transitional phase in Mughal architecture, from the red sandstone architecture of Akbar towards the style of Shah Jahan's reign.

quotes.quote: The mausoleum is like a jewel box: built entirely of pure marble, it marks the transitional phase from the grand and massive red sandstone architecture of Akbar to the softer and sensual architectural style that marked the reign of Shah Jahan.

quotes.locator: The Jewel Box of Mughal India
quotes.quote: Before the Taj Mahal, the tomb of Itmad-ud-Daula in Agra (1621-1627 CE) marked a turning point in Mughal architecture.

It marks a transitional phase in Mughal architecture from the red sandstone and marble decoration of the monuments of Akbar's era, such as Humayun's Tomb and Akbar's tomb, to the white marble and pietra dura inlay exemplified by the Taj Mahal of Shah Jahan.

claims.text: Live History India dates the tomb of Itimad-ud-Daulah in Agra to 1621-1627 CE.

quotes.locator: The Jewel Box of Mughal India
quotes.quote: Before the Taj Mahal, the tomb of Itmad-ud-Daula in Agra (1621-1627 CE) marked a turning point in Mughal architecture.

claims.text: Archnet and Wikipedia date the tomb of Itimad-ud-Daulah to 1622-1628, Archnet saying Nur Jahan commissioned it on her father's death in 1622.

quotes.quote: His daughter, Nur Jahan, later married the Emperor and commissioned the mausoleum to honor the memory of her father upon his death in 1622.
Built between 1622 and 1628, it was commissioned by the Mughal empress Nur Jahan for her father

claims.text: Pietra dura first appeared in Rome in the 16th century, where the V&A says the ancient Roman technique of inlaying coloured stones was revived in the 1550s.

quotes.quote: It first appeared in Rome in the 16th century, reaching its full maturity in Florence.

The technique of creating inlays from coloured stones was practised by the ancient Romans and revived in the 1550s in Rome, where recent archaeological excavations meant that there were abundant supplies of antique marbles to be found.

claims.text: Gems & Gemology says most historians credit the Italians with creating pietra dura in Florence, where it was called commesso di pietre dure, 'composition of hard stones'.

quotes.quote: Most historians credit the Italians with creating this technique in Florence, where it was called commesso di pietre dure ("composition of hard stones") and often abbreviated to pietra dura
Said to have been originally developed and perfected by Florentine artists in sixteenth-century Italy

claims.text: The Mughals had received gifts of decorative objects with inlay from Italy and had acquired an appreciation for the art.

quotes.quote: The Mughals had received gifts from Italy of decorative objects with inlay and had acquired an appreciation for the art.

claims.text: Gems & Gemology states that European artists brought the pietra dura technique with them to India to work on the Taj Mahal.

quotes.quote: European artists brought the technique with them to India to work on the Taj Mahal.

claims.text: Gems & Gemology also states that parchin kari developed independently in India and entered the monuments of the Mughal empire during the sixteenth century.

quotes.locator: History of the Families that Performed the Inlay
quotes.quote: The tradition of fine stone inlay, or parchin kari, developed independently in India and began to be incorporated into the monuments of the Mughal empire during the sixteenth century.

claims.text: Outlook Traveller reports that Shah Jahan brought pietra dura to India in the 17th century, with experts from Persia, when he commissioned the Taj Mahal.

quotes.quote: The art of Pietra Dura, as it was called in Italy, was brought to India in the 17th century by the Mughal emperor Shah Jahan when he commissioned the Taj Mahal and brought experts from Persia
The art was brought to India in the 17th century from Persia when Shah Jahan chose to build the Taj Mahal.

claims.text: Live History India says the craft of marble inlay journeyed to India in the 16th century and was transformed under Mughal patronage into parchin kari.

quotes.locator: From Rome to the Mughal Courts
quotes.quote: In the 16th century, this craft journeyed to India, where it underwent a remarkable transformation under Mughal patronage, becoming the uniquely Indian art of parchin kari.

claims.text: The western pietra dura technique adapted for the Taj Mahal's inlaid flowers is believed to have been imported to the Mughal court during Jahangir's reign.

quotes.quote: These decorative patterns, found throughout the tomb, were created by adapting the western pietra dura technique, believed to have been imported to the court during the reign of the emperor Jahangir.

claims.text: Some scholars believe Italian artisans taught local artisans in Mughal workshops, while others think local artisans skilled in softer-stone inlay might have learnt it themselves.

quotes.quote: Some scholars believe that Italian artisans taught local artisans at Mughal workshops, while others think that local artisans might have learnt it themselves since they were already skilled in inlay techniques that employed softer stones.
While we still do not know which of these versions is true

claims.text: For a time before Lord Curzon's restoration of the Taj Mahal was completed in 1908, security was not stringent and some stones of its pietra dura were stolen.

quotes.locator: The Taj Mahal Today and Its Conservation
quotes.quote: For a time up until the restoration by British Viceroy Lord Curzon was completed in 1908, security was not stringent, so some of the stones in the pietra dura as well as other decor were stolen

claims.text: As Mughal power declined in the 18th century and royal patronage waned, parchin kari artisans began making tabletops and jewellery boxes for European buyers.

quotes.locator: The Decline of a Glorious Craft
quotes.quote: The decline of Mughal power in the 18th century marked a turning point for parchin kari. As royal patronage waned, artisans began creating decorative items like tabletops and jewelry boxes for European buyers, who were enchanted by the intricate craftsmanship.

claims.text: The parchinkari craftsmen of Agra are believed to be descendants of the craftsmen who built the Taj Mahal.

quotes.quote: The Parchinkari craftsmen of Agra are believed to be descendants of the same craftsmen who built the Taj Mahal.
The craftsmen who are predominantly Muslim, are said to be descendants of those same craftsmen.

claims.text: A design magazine reports that the Taj Mahal's inlay artisans passed their skills to later generations, but only to the men and only within the family.

quotes.quote: Fortunately, the artisans were still able to pass on their skills to future generations (although only to the men and only within the family)

claims.text: It is said that the most skilled workers on the Taj Mahal had one hand cut off after it was finished so they could never repeat the work.

quotes.quote: It is said that the most skilled individuals who had worked on the Taj Mahal had one hand cut off after it was finished so they could never duplicate this work again.

claims.text: An Italian or Italian-inspired pietra dura tablet of Orpheus, dated 1648, is set into the back wall of Shah Jahan's throne at the Diwan-i-Aam of the Red Fort in Delhi, with 318 other inlay panels.

quotes.quote: an Italian or Italian-inspired pietra dura panel appearing in a Mughal context is that of a tablet, dating to 1648, depicting the Greek mythological figure, Orpheus, set into the back wall of Shah Jahan's throne at the Diwan-i-Aam in the Red Fort in Delhi, along with 318 other panels of inlay.

claims.text: The Hindu calls Makrana the oldest among Indian cities with marble quarries.

quotes.quote: Makrana is the oldest among cities in India with marble quarries.

claims.text: A master artist plans each design, dividing the marble panel into systematic sections with traditional geometric tools and making a final sketch at 1:1 scale.

quotes.quote: The master artist who is a thoroughly knowledgeable person plans the each design. Marble panel is divided in systematic sections using traditional geometric tools and making final sketch of the selected design on 1:1 Scale.

claims.text: The whole drawing is traced on a brass sheet, which a specialist cuts out accurately to make templates of every component of the design.

quotes.quote: The entire drawing is traced on a brass sheet, which is cut out accurately by a specialist to make templates of every component of the design.
The craftsman matches the shapes to a brass template.

claims.text: Choosing the design involves setting its colour scheme and tonality and choosing different stones by their shades.

quotes.quote: Which involves choosing a design, setting a colour scheme and tonality of the design and choosing different types of stones based on their shades to be used in the product.

claims.text: Base stones and inlay stones are sourced to suit the design, and the base stone may be white or black marble or soapstone.

quotes.quote: Based on the design, base stones and inlay stones are sourced. The base stone may be white or black marble or soapstone.

claims.text: Gems & Gemology says that in advanced inlays a bow saw coated with abrasives was used to fashion the slivers of gem material.

quotes.quote: In advanced inlays, slivers of different gem materials were artfully placed in the space with a view toward creating colors and shapes of the desired geometric patterns or floral designs. A bow saw coated with abrasives was used to fashion the slivers (figure 19).

claims.text: The inlay stones are cut and shaped to the design on an emery wheel, and because each part is shaped individually the work is time consuming.

quotes.quote: The stone to be inlayed are cut and given the desired shape as per the design using a special instrument called emery wheel. Since each part of the design is shaped individually, it is time consuming.
Stone slivers are carefully shaped into minute petals, leaves, and stems on a manually operated emery wheel.
Each shape is ground individually and must fit precisely without any gaps.

claims.text: Lapidaries shape the gemstones on a hand-driven tool called Saan & Kamaani, holding tiny pieces in their fingertips against an emery wheel turned by a cane rod with a leather band.

quotes.quote: This begins with lapidary artists who shape the selected gem stones on a hand driven tool known as "Saan & Kamaani".
tiny pieces of gemstones are held in the fingertips and touched with emery wheel, which is rotated by hand with great precision using a cane rod attached with a leather band.

claims.text: A design magazine reports that, at the cooperative its writer visited in India, the artisan makes delicate shapes, some only a few millimetres in size, from thin stone sheets using only a human-powered grindstone.

quotes.quote: On a recent trip to India, I had the chance to learn how these stone inlays are made.
The artisans work together as a cooperative, meaning each of them remains an individual artist with complete creative freedom, but all profits are shared equally.
The starting point are thin sheets of various (semiprecious) stone, from which the artisan creates delicate shapes, some only a few millimetres in size
Only a (human-powered) grindstone is used

claims.text: The design magazine reports that each individually ground stone shape must fit precisely, without any gaps.

quotes.quote: Each shape is ground individually and must fit precisely without any gaps.

claims.text: In the method Gems & Gemology describes, a master artist known as the parchinkar would first draw the pattern in henna dye on the marble's surface.

quotes.quote: A master artist known as the parchinkar would first draw the pattern in henna dye on the marble's surface.

claims.text: In the design magazine's account, once the pieces fit, the marble plate is covered with henna paint, the pieces are laid on it and their outlines scratched in, and the orange colour guides the carving of the grooves.

quotes.quote: Once a perfect fit has been achieved, the marble plate, into which the ornamental pattern will be integrated, is covered with a layer of henna paint.

The single pieces that make the inlay pattern are laid out on the marble plate and their outlines scratched into the surface. The orange color serves as an orientation when carving out the individual grooves, into which the semiprecious stone pieces will be glued.

claims.text: In the GI application's method, craftsmen trace the design onto the base stone using a sharp tool.

quotes.quote: Craftsmen trace the design onto the base stone using a sharp tool.

claims.text: Grooves are cut into the base stone with a chisel so that the shaped stones fit them perfectly.

quotes.quote: Grooves are cut into the design in the base stone using a chisel such that the shaped stone can perfectly fit in them.
Artisans, known as parachinkars, carve intricate grooves into marble, into which semi-precious stones are carefully inlaid.

claims.text: For a marble inlay artefact the marble is chiselled with a diamond-tipped chisel, while the stones are cut and shaped with a hand-operated machine.

quotes.quote: To make a marble inlay artefact, the stones are cut and shaped with a hand-operated machine while the marble is chiselled with a diamond-tipped chisel.

claims.text: The GI application says the stones are inlaid into the grooves with glue, by traditional methods using charcoal or modern ones using araldite.

quotes.quote: Once the grooves are cut, the stones are inlayed into the base stone using glue. Traditional methods like charcoal or modern methods like araldite are being used.
The stone is then pressed into place and fixed with a burning charcoal.

claims.text: A design magazine reports that the glue still in use is a paste made from sugar cane, beeswax, honey, lemon juice, marble dust and lentils.

quotes.quote: the glue in use is still a paste made from sugar cane, bees wax, honey, lemon juice, marble dust and lentils.

claims.text: The carved space is filled with thin polished pieces of gem material fixed with organic glue, grooved to fit together so that the joins are almost invisible.

quotes.quote: Then the artist would carve out a space in the marble and fill it with thin polished pieces of gem materials, affixing them with organic glue.
The stones were grooved so they would fit together, making the contact between them almost invisible. The technique is still used to this day

claims.text: Outlook Traveller found the exact recipe of the adhesive that holds the stones hard to figure out, and the artisans claim it is a trade secret.

quotes.quote: held in place using an adhesive (the exact recipe for which is hard to figure out. It&rsquos a trade secret, the artisans claim)

claims.text: Once inlaid, the stones are left for some time to dry so that they are properly pasted.

quotes.quote: Once inlayed, the stones need to be left for some time for drying so that they are properly pasted.

claims.text: The piece is hand polished with a traditional polishing powder on a soft moist muslin cloth, and the final polishing is done with zinc powder.

quotes.quote: Hand polishing of the base article is done using a traditional polishing powder which is applied on the surface with a soft moist muslin cloth.
The final polishing is done using zink powder.
The final polishing is done with zinc power.

claims.text: Grinding and polishing is a multi-stage process using graded grits of hard stone, followed by continuous rubbing with pigments and wax.

quotes.quote: Grinding and polishing is a multi stage process, using graded grit of hard stone, followed by continuous rubbing with pigments and wax.

claims.text: After the inlays are inserted, a grindstone shard smooths the surface and removes the henna, and the piece gets a final finish with a layer of wax.

quotes.quote: A grind stone shard is used to smoothen the surface after the inlays have been inserted.
The henna paint is also removed during this smoothening process. The inlay piece is now properly integrated into the marble plate, and gets a final finish with a layer of wax.

claims.text: Agra stone inlay has two categories of artisans: Sadakars do basic cutting and carving aided by machines, and Pachikars do the exclusive inlay work.

quotes.quote: There are two categories of artisans- Sadakars and Pachikars.

While basic cutting and carving aided by machines is done by skilled Sadakars, exclusive inlay work, requiring the expertise similar to cutting and polishing of jewelry stones using chisels and grinding stones is done by experienced Pachikars.

claims.text: Agra artisans use country-made machines for cutting, grinding, buffing and polishing stone, yet curvilinear designs still need skilful handling of chisel and hammer.

glossary.meaning: The art of inlaying coloured or semi-precious stones into a stone base, often in geometric or flower patterns; in Mughal India the name of pietra dura, literally 'driven in'.
Italian for 'hard stone': a technique in which precious and semi-precious stones are cut, polished and inlaid, generally on hard stone such as marble, to represent an image.
The inlay artisan: the experienced craftsman who does the exclusive inlay work and carves the grooves into which the stones are inlaid.
An artisan who does the basic cutting and carving of the stone, aided by machines.
The hand-driven tool on which lapidaries shape the gemstones against an emery wheel turned by a cane rod with a leather band.
Flat chisel, used to carve out the fine details on the surface of the marble.
Cold chisel, used to cut through the raw marble slab to the basic shape of the product.
Hammer, used to drive the chisel through the raw marble for sculpting and carving.
Pen drill, used to make rough outlines of the patterns on the marble and to carve the designs.
Divider, used to draw outlines as concentric circles for geometric patterns.
'Composition of hard stones', the Florentine name for the technique, often abbreviated to pietra dura.

lede.text: Agra marble inlay, also called parchin kari or pachhikari, is the art of inlaying semi-precious stones into a marble base, a technique that dates back to the Mughal era.
The GI application names Nai Ki Mandi, Taj Ganj and the areas around the Taj Mahal in Agra as its main areas, and Live History India and Outlook Traveller report it around Fatehpur Sikri too.
Pachikars do the inlay work, with stones such as agate, turquoise, cornelian, jasper, mother of pearl, malachite and lapis lazuli, and stone items are made from Makrana marble among other stones.
The craft reached its peak under the Mughals, especially after the Taj Mahal was built, and Agra Stone Inlay Craft is a registered geographical indication with a certificate dated 27 March 2025.

keyFacts.label: Centres
keyFacts.value: Nai Ki Mandi, Taj Ganj and around the Taj Mahal in Agra (GI application); Fatehpur Sikri, press reports say

keyFacts.label: Artisans
keyFacts.value: Pachikars do the inlay; Sadakars do machine-aided cutting and carving

keyFacts.label: Base stones
keyFacts.value: White or black marble or soapstone; white marble from Makrana, a calcitic marble of Nagaur District, Rajasthan

keyFacts.label: Inlay stones
keyFacts.value: Agate, turquoise, cornelian, jasper, mother of pearl, malachite, lapis lazuli, black marble, coral

keyFacts.label: Fixing
keyFacts.value: Sources differ: glue by charcoal or araldite (GI application), or a paste of sugar cane, beeswax, honey, lemon juice, marble dust and lentils (a design magazine)

keyFacts.label: Designs
keyFacts.value: Floral, geometric and nature-inspired; over 2000 designs, the GI application says

sentences.text: Humayun is credited with introducing inlay as a significant feature of Mughal architecture, and the Qila-i-Kuhna Mosque of 1540 CE in Delhi's Purana Qila shows one of the earliest examples of inlay work in India.

Sources differ on where pietra dura began: in Rome, where the V&A dates the revival of the ancient Roman stone inlay to the 1550s, or in Florence, where Gems & Gemology says most historians credit its creation.

The tomb of Itimad-ud-Daulah in Agra, commissioned by Nur Jahan for her father and dated by sources to 1621-1627 CE or 1622-1628, is considered the first Mughal structure built entirely of white marble and marks a transitional phase in Mughal architecture.

Sources differ on how the technique reached India: Gems & Gemology states both that European artists brought it and that parchin kari developed independently in India, Outlook Traveller credits Shah Jahan and experts from Persia in the 17th century, and Live History India dates its arrival to the 16th century.
Sources also differ on when building of the Taj Mahal began, in 1630, 1631, 1632 or 1633, and the mausoleum was completed in 1648 and the whole complex in 1653.
Inlayers, stone-cutters and calligraphers were requisitioned from across the empire and from Central Asia and Iran, and more than 20,000 craftsmen and workers are believed to have been employed.

As royal patronage waned in the 18th century, artisans began making tabletops and jewellery boxes for European buyers, and after the British conquest of Agra inlay souvenirs found willing buyers and a whole industry came to life.
The GI application says the sequence of processes was perfected in the 17th century and has remained largely unchanged for over 400 years.
A master artist plans each design, makes a final sketch at 1:1 scale and traces it on a brass sheet that a specialist cuts into templates of every component.
Gems & Gemology says a bow saw coated with abrasives was used to fashion the slivers of gem material, and the GI application has each part of the design shaped individually on an emery wheel.
On the hand-driven Saan & Kamaani, lapidaries hold tiny pieces in their fingertips against an emery wheel turned by a cane rod with a leather band.

In Gems & Gemology's account the parchinkar would first draw the pattern in henna dye on the marble, the GI application has the design traced onto the base stone with a sharp tool, and grooves are cut with a chisel so that the shaped stones fit them perfectly.
Sources differ on the fixing: the GI application names glue by charcoal or araldite, while a design magazine reports a paste of sugar cane, beeswax, honey, lemon juice, marble dust and lentils.
Once inlaid, the stones are left to dry, the piece is hand polished with a traditional powder on a moist muslin cloth, and the final polishing is done with zinc powder.
Sadakars do the basic cutting and carving aided by machines, and Pachikars do the exclusive inlay work.
Agate, turquoise, cornelian, jasper, mother of pearl, malachite, lapis lazuli and black marble are used in marble inlay in Agra.

The GI application describes lapis lazuli as a vivid blue stone prized for its intense colour, carnelian as a bright reddish-orange stone often used in floral patterns, malachite as a striking green stone with swirling patterns, and coral as used for accenting designs.
Agra stone handicrafts are also made from soapstones such as selam, gorara and palewa and from alabaster, and gold or silver foil sometimes gives inlaid items a luxurious finish.
The Taj Mahal's white marble was brought from the Makrana quarries in Rajasthan, nearly 400 km from Agra.
Sources differ on how many stone materials the Taj Mahal holds, 28 or over 40, brought from places including China, Tibet, Afghanistan and Sri Lanka.
Gems & Gemology describes its Koranic inscriptions as black onyx inlay, while PBS describes them as black marble.
Makrana marble is a calcitic marble from the Makrana and Parbatsar tehsils of Nagaur District, and with Sirohi marble the only calcitic marble of India.
Its deposits belong to the Ajmer Formation of the Kumbhalgarh Group of the Delhi Supergroup, and its marble bands formed through tight isoclinal folding.
The Makrana Marble GI application says the close interlocking of its grains gives it strength, hardness and translucency, and gives its water absorption as 0.04%, the lowest among calcitic marbles.

Sources differ on whether the marble occurs in five or six bands, which the GI journal says extend over 20 kilometres, while the quarries that supplied the Taj Mahal stretched more than 22 km and the 1997-98 mine cluster about 13 km.
The International Union of Geological Sciences lists Makrana marble as a Global Heritage Stone Resource, the first from India and Asia.
The cut stones are inlaid into the marble base to create floral, geometric and nature-inspired patterns, and a single flower or leaf is often made of different pieces of stone.
The GI application says over 2000 designs are visible in Agra stone inlay work.
Outlook Traveller says the mark of a fine piece of inlay work is that the precious stone seems to have grown out of the marble.
Ebba Koch says flowers were central to the Taj Mahal's decoration because they symbolised the flora of Paradise, and some depict real lilies, tulips and poppy blossoms.
Koch judges that the complexity, subtlety and elegance of the work of Shah Jahan's lapidaries far surpasses that of the Italian artists.
Application 661 for Agra Stone Inlay Work was filed by the Handicrafts Exporter's Association on 30 September 2019 and registered with certificate 659 dated 27 March 2025.
An earlier application, 216 for Agra Marble Inlay Work, filed on 2 September 2010, was withdrawn.

The GI application reports a lot of demand for marble inlay products at home and in western countries, and the Taj Mahal's floral ornamentation has inspired an entire industry of marble souvenirs and stone-inlaid objects in Agra.
The V&A records that around 1860-70 Agra craftsmen made small portable artefacts for the many tourists visiting the Taj Mahal, and also inlaid table tops and chess boards.
Live History India reports that the labour-intensive work and a lack of lucrative opportunities have led many young artisans to abandon the trade.
The GI application calls alabaster and gorahari stone hot and harmful for the artisan, while selam stone is not harmful.
The GI application says palawa stone gives off heavy and harmful dust.
A design magazine reports that a craftsman shaping stones on a human-powered grindstone inevitably also abrades the skin on his fingers.
